summary: Defines a MIME content type for holding directory information, such as the details of people or organizations. It gives a general text format that profiles like vCard build on. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 6350.

eli5.summary: It is a standard way to write contact information so any program can read it, like a neat card file that all programs agree on.

questions: what is the mime directory content type
what format does vcard build on
how to represent directory information in mime
how to extend text directory types
subtitle: A standard text format for structuring directory information in email messages.

tldr.problem: Organizations and email systems needed a standard way to exchange structured directory information like contact details, but there was no agreed format that worked across different directory services and protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2425 defines a MIME content type called text/directory using a simple property-value format where each line has a type name, optional parameters, a colon, and a value. It includes a framework for defining custom types, parameters, and value formats through a registration process.
tldr.outcome: Other specifications like vCard (used for contact information) and iCalendar (used for calendar events) build on this foundation. It was later updated by RFC 6350 with refinements, but the core approach remains in wide use.

today: RFC 6350 later superseded RFC 2425 with updates to vCard and directory handling, but the core text/directory framework defined here remains the foundation for contact information exchange. The format continues to be widely used in vCard and similar applications.

sections.title: Why a MIME Directory Format
sections.content:
Email users and applications needed to exchange directory information—address books, business cards, contacts—but different systems used different formats. The text/directory content type solves this by defining a standard text-based format that any email system can handle.

Unlike specialized directory protocols like LDAP or X.500, the text/directory approach works everywhere email works, making it easy to send contact information between systems that have never met before. It is also designed to be human-readable and easy to parse.
sections.eli5: Email systems wanted a standard way to send contact information. RFC 2425 says: use simple lines that say what type of info each line holds (like NAME or EMAIL), then a colon, then the value.

sections.title: The Basic Format
sections.content:
Each line in a text/directory body follows the pattern: TYPE:value. Optional parameters can appear between the type and the colon, separated by semicolons. For example: NAME:John Doe or EMAIL;TYPE=INTERNET:john@example.com.

Long lines can be folded across multiple physical lines by inserting a space after a line break. Type names are case-insensitive (NAME and name mean the same thing), but some parameter values may be case-sensitive. The format uses UTF-8 as the preferred character encoding.
sections.eli5: Each line starts with a type name, then a colon, then the value. You can add extra information in the middle separated by semicolons. Long lines can wrap to the next line with a space at the start.

sections.title: Types, Values, and Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines a framework where applications can create new types (like NAME, EMAIL, PHONE) and new value types (like text, date, integer, URI). Each value type has a specific format; for example, dates follow ISO 8601 format and text values use backslash escapes for commas and newlines.

Parameters modify how a value should be interpreted—for example, TYPE=WORK indicates a work email address, or LANGUAGE=fr indicates French text. Parameters are optional; applications that do not recognize them can simply ignore them.

The RFC defines basic types like SOURCE (location of the information), NAME (a descriptive name), and PROFILE (indicating which profile—like vCard—is being used). It also allows vendor-specific types starting with x- for experimental or proprietary use.
sections.eli5: You can invent new types of information (like PHONE or ADDRESS) and tell the system how to format them (as text, as a date, as a number). You can add hints about each value, like TYPE=WORK to say it is a work email.

sections.title: Profiles and Extensibility
sections.content:
The RFC is designed to be a foundation that other specifications can build on. A profile is a set of types and rules for a particular use case. For example, vCard (RFC 2426) is a profile that defines how to represent a person's contact information using the text/directory format.

New profiles, types, parameters, and value types are registered with IANA through a defined process. This allows the system to grow without breaking existing implementations. Applications that encounter unknown types or parameters can choose to ignore them gracefully, making the format forward-compatible.
sections.eli5: This RFC is like a recipe template: other RFCs (like vCard) use it as a base and add specific rules for contact cards. Different specifications can register their own types without breaking each other.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The text/directory format itself does not define encryption or access control. Directory information in one system may be protected, but once it is sent as text/directory format, protection depends on how it is transmitted (for example, using TLS for email or signing/encrypting with MIME security mechanisms).

The format does not include integrity or privacy guarantees, so applications should use MIME-based security mechanisms (like S/MIME) when exchanging sensitive information. Unlike some directory protocols, it does not have built-in authentication of the sender.
sections.eli5: This format itself does not protect information—if you send contact details, anyone who sees the email can read them. Use email encryption if the information is private.

sections.title: Practical Use
sections.content:
The most common use is in vCard format for contact information. A simple vCard might contain: BEGIN:VCARD, N:Doe;John, EMAIL:john@example.com, PHONE:+1-555-1234, and END:VCARD. The RFC also defines how to include non-textual information (photos, sound files) by using the multipart/related MIME type to attach them alongside the text/directory body part.

Profiles define which types are required, which are optional, and what order they should appear in. An application reading a vCard, for example, knows exactly which fields to expect and how to interpret them.
sections.eli5: vCard is the most common use: it lists a person's name, email, phone, and address in the text/directory format. You can also attach photos or sounds by including them as separate attachments.
